questions.q: On an 802.1Q trunk, how does a receiving switch treat a frame that arrives without a VLAN tag?

choices.text: It assumes the frame belongs to the native VLAN
choices.why: Native VLAN frames cross a trunk untagged, so a receiving switch assigns any untagged frame on a trunk to the native VLAN (VLAN 1 by default).

choices.text: It forwards the frame to the parking-lot VLAN
choices.why: The parking-lot VLAN is an unused VLAN that unused, shut-down ports are assigned to. It has nothing to do with untagged trunk frames.

choices.text: It floods the frame to every VLAN on the trunk
choices.why: A switch never floods one frame into all VLANs; the untagged frame is placed only in the native VLAN.

choices.text: It drops the frame as a VLAN hopping attempt
choices.why: Untagged frames are expected on a trunk for the native VLAN. VLAN hopping is an attacker tagging frames with arbitrary VLANs after gaining a trunk.

questions.q: Four switches all use the default STP bridge priority. Which switch becomes the root bridge?

choices.text: The switch with the most trunk ports
choices.why: The number of trunks plays no part in the root election, which compares only bridge IDs (priority plus MAC).

choices.text: The switch with the highest MAC address
choices.why: In STP lower is always preferred. The highest MAC address would lose the election.

choices.text: The switch with the lowest port cost
choices.why: Port cost is used to choose root ports toward the root bridge after it is elected, not to elect the root itself.

choices.text: The switch with the lowest MAC address
choices.why: The bridge ID is priority plus base MAC address and the lowest bridge ID wins, so with equal priorities the lowest MAC address decides.

questions.q: A user unplugs a PC and connects a small unmanaged switch that starts sending BPDUs on an access port. Which feature shuts the port down so the user cannot change the STP topology?

choices.text: BPDU Guard
choices.why: BPDU Guard err-disables an access port when a BPDU arrives, since end users never send legitimate BPDUs.

choices.text: Storm Control
choices.why: Storm Control limits the amount of broadcast or multicast traffic through the switch. It does not react to BPDUs.

choices.text: Root Guard
choices.why: Root Guard keeps a port from becoming a root port toward a new remote root switch. It is meant for ports to switches you don't manage, not for blocking every BPDU on access ports.

choices.text: PortFast
choices.why: PortFast makes a host port skip listening and learning and go straight to forwarding. It does not shut down a port that receives BPDUs.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: What is the default port security violation mode on a Cisco switch port?

choices.text: Restrict, which drops frames and sends syslog
choices.why: Restrict drops frames over the limit and also generates a syslog message. It is an optional mode, not the default.

choices.text: Shutdown, which err-disables the port
choices.why: Shutdown is the default violation action. The port is placed in the err-disabled state when the MAC limit is exceeded.

choices.text: Protect, which drops frames from new MACs
choices.why: Protect keeps the port up and silently drops frames from MACs over the limit, but it must be configured; it is not the default.

choices.text: Sticky, which writes MACs to the configuration
choices.why: Sticky is not a violation mode. It is a port security option that writes dynamically learned MACs into the running configuration.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets on untrusted ports against which source of information?

choices.text: The IPv6 first-hop security binding table
choices.why: The first-hop security binding table validates IPv6 neighbors. DAI is an IPv4 ARP feature that relies on DHCP snooping bindings.

choices.text: The CAM table of the switch
choices.why: The CAM table is the switch's MAC address table used for forwarding. DAI does not use it to validate IP-to-MAC bindings.

choices.text: The CEF table with receive adjacencies
choices.why: The CEF table is the router's forwarding table; receive entries mark traffic destined to the device itself. It is not used for ARP validation.

choices.text: The DHCP snooping binding database
choices.why: DAI checks IP-to-MAC bindings against the DHCP snooping binding database, which exists only when DHCP snooping is enabled on the switch and VLANs.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: According to Network Foundation Protection, OSPF and EIGRP routing updates exchanged between routers belong to which plane?

choices.text: Services plane
choices.why: NFP divides the infrastructure into management, control, and data planes. Routing protocols are explicitly a control plane function.

choices.text: Control plane
choices.why: The control plane covers protocols that devices run on their own, such as routing protocols. A failure there means the router can't learn or share routes.

choices.text: Data plane
choices.why: The data plane is transit traffic forwarded through the device between clients and servers, not routing updates to the router itself.

choices.text: Management plane
choices.why: The management plane is traffic between an administrator and the device, such as SSH, not routing protocol exchanges.

questions.q: Which syslog severity level number corresponds to Warnings?

choices.why: Level 3 is Error (error conditions), one step more severe than Warnings.
Level 2 is Critical, for critical conditions.
Level 4 is Warnings (warning conditions), between level 3 Error and level 5 Notifications.
Level 5 is Notifications, for normal but significant conditions.

questions.q: Which transport protocol and port does NTP use?

choices.text: UDP 123
choices.why: NTP synchronizes device clocks over UDP port 123.

choices.text: UDP 161
choices.why: UDP 161 is SNMP, used to read and change device information; traps use UDP 162.

choices.text: UDP 514
choices.why: UDP 514 is syslog, which sends log messages in plain text by default.

choices.text: TCP 123
choices.why: NTP runs over UDP, not TCP. Port 123 is correct only with UDP.

questions.section: 4. Understanding and Securing the Management Plane

questions.q: An engineer types crypto key generate rsa on a new router that still has its factory hostname and no other changes, and the command fails. What must be configured first?

choices.text: The ip ssh version 2 command and a vty password
choices.why: ip ssh version 2 enables SSHv2 and vty login is needed for SSH sessions, but neither is a prerequisite for generating the RSA keys.

choices.text: The ip http secure-server command
choices.why: ip http secure-server enables HTTPS management and generates its own keys. It is not required before crypto key generate rsa.

choices.text: The aaa new-model command and a TACACS+ server
choices.why: AAA can be used for SSH login, but the key generation command depends only on a hostname and domain name.

choices.text: A hostname other than Router and a domain name
choices.why: The RSA key pair is named from the hostname and domain name, so key generation fails until a non-default hostname and ip domain-name are set.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes NETCONF?

choices.text: It runs over SSH, uses YANG models, and encodes data in XML
choices.why: NETCONF runs over SSH, uses YANG data models, encodes configuration data in XML, and supports atomic transactions.

choices.text: It runs over gRPC and uses Protocol Buffers messages
choices.why: gNMI uses gRPC as its transport, and the book's gNMI example is written in Protocol Buffers syntax. That describes gNMI, not NETCONF.

choices.text: It runs over HTTPS and uses MIB community strings
choices.why: RESTCONF is the YANG-based protocol that runs over HTTPS. Community strings belong to SNMP, which neither NETCONF nor RESTCONF uses.

choices.text: It runs over UDP and sends unsolicited traps
choices.why: Unsolicited traps over UDP describe SNMP. NETCONF uses a secure SSH session.

questions.q: An IPv6 address that begins with FE80 and is created automatically on an interface when none is configured is which type of address?

choices.text: Solicited-node multicast address
choices.why: Solicited-node multicast addresses have the form FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx and are joined for each unicast address. They are multicast, not FE80 addresses.

choices.text: Anycast address
choices.why: An anycast address is one that appears more than once in the network, with the network choosing the best one. It is not defined by an FE80 prefix.

choices.text: Link-local address
choices.why: Link-local addresses begin with FE80, are used only on the local network, and are created automatically if not configured.

choices.text: Global unicast address
choices.why: Global unicast addresses are routable and start in the 2000 to 3FFF range, not FE80.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: How does modified EUI-64 build a 64-bit interface ID from a 48-bit MAC address?

choices.text: It prepends FE80 and appends the MAC unchanged
choices.why: FE80 is the link-local prefix, which is separate from the interface ID. The MAC is not used unchanged, because FFFE is inserted and a bit is inverted.

choices.text: It appends FFFE to the end of the MAC address
choices.why: FFFE goes in the middle of the MAC address, not at the end, and the seventh bit is also inverted.

choices.text: It inserts FFFE in the middle and inverts the seventh bit
choices.why: Modified EUI-64 splits the MAC, inserts FFFE in the middle, and inverts the seventh bit from the left, which is why CA becomes C8 in the book's example.

choices.text: It copies the last 24 bits of the MAC after FF02::1:FF
choices.why: FF02::1:FF plus the last 24 bits describes the solicited-node multicast address, not how an interface ID is built.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: In a CoPP classification ACL, what does a permit statement mean?

choices.text: Matching traffic is logged with log-input
choices.why: The book warns never to use log or log-input in CoPP ACLs because they can cause unexpected results.

choices.text: Matching traffic is inspected by that class
choices.why: ACL logic in CoPP is reversed from normal filtering: permit means the traffic matches and is handled by that class's policy.

choices.text: Matching traffic skips the class and cascades
choices.why: That is what deny means in a CoPP ACL: the traffic skips that class and moves on to the next class, if one exists.

choices.text: Matching traffic always reaches the CPU unpoliced
choices.why: Permit only places traffic in the class. What happens next depends on the policy action, which may police or drop it.

questions.section: 12. Securing Routing Protocols and the Control Plane

questions.q: Which pair of routing protocols in the chapter uses a globally configured key chain for MD5 authentication?

choices.text: BGP and RIPv1
choices.why: BGP's basic MD5 uses the neighbor password option, and RIPv1 does not support authentication at all.

choices.text: OSPF and EIGRP
choices.why: EIGRP uses a key chain, but OSPF does not; OSPF uses ip ospf message-digest-key on the interface or area authentication in the process.

choices.text: EIGRP and RIPv2
choices.why: EIGRP and RIPv2 reference a global key chain with numbered keys and key strings, applied per interface.

choices.text: OSPF and BGP
choices.why: Neither uses a key chain in the book's basic examples: OSPF uses message-digest-key and BGP uses the neighbor password command.

questions.section: 12. Securing Routing Protocols and the Control Plane

questions.q: A help desk team must be able to run only ping, show commands, and access-list configuration on a router. Which feature creates a named subset of commands that many users can share for this?

choices.text: Login Password Retry Lockout
choices.why: This feature locks a local AAA account after a set number of failed logins. It does not define a command subset.

choices.text: Service password encryption
choices.why: Service password encryption only scrambles plaintext passwords in the configuration (type 7). It does not restrict commands.

choices.text: Cisco Resilient Configuration
choices.why: Resilient Configuration protects the IOS image and startup configuration from deletion. It does not limit which commands a user can run.

choices.text: A parser view
choices.why: A parser view is a named subset of commands; users placed in the view can use only those commands, and many users can share one view.

questions.q: What does privilege level 15 represent on a Cisco IOS device?

choices.text: Privileged mode, reached with the enable command
choices.why: Level 15 is privileged mode, entered with enable, and nearly all configuration commands belong to it by default.

choices.text: The root view used to create parser views
choices.why: The root view is entered with enable view and the enable secret. It is a parser view concept, not a privilege level number.

choices.text: A custom level with commands moved down
choices.why: Custom levels are 2 to 14, created by moving commands down from level 15.

choices.text: User mode, with a prompt ending in >
choices.why: User mode is privilege level 1, not level 15.

questions.q: With default 802.1D timers, about how long does a newly connected switch port take to begin forwarding?

choices.text: 20 seconds
choices.why: 20 seconds is the max age timer, which a blocked port can add on top of the 30-second startup delay.

choices.text: 15 seconds
choices.why: 15 seconds is the forward delay for one state only. The port passes through both listening and learning.

choices.text: 30 seconds
choices.why: A new port spends 15 seconds listening and 15 seconds learning, a total of 30 seconds before forwarding.

choices.text: 2 seconds
choices.why: 2 seconds is the STP hello timer, the interval between BPDUs.

questions.q: Hosts on an access VLAN are receiving a false default gateway from a device that pretends to be a legitimate IPv6 router. Which switch feature blocks or rejects these rogue router advertisements?

choices.text: IPv6 Destination Guard
choices.why: Destination Guard blocks data traffic to unidentified destinations and defends against neighbor cache resource starvation, not rogue RAs.

choices.text: IPv6 RA Guard
choices.why: IPv6 RA Guard blocks or rejects rogue router advertisements at the switch, preventing the man-in-the-middle they enable.

choices.text: IPv6 device tracking
choices.why: Device tracking lets the IPv6 neighbor table reflect immediately when a host becomes inactive. It does not filter router advertisements.

choices.text: Dynamic ARP Inspection
choices.why: DAI validates IPv4 ARP packets. IPv6 has no ARP, and rogue router advertisements are handled by RA Guard.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: What is the maximum number of methods an AAA method list can contain?

choices.text: Sixteen
choices.why: Sixteen is far beyond the limit of four. The number 16 appears elsewhere, for example EIGRP maximum paths.

choices.text: Eight
choices.why: Eight exceeds the limit. The method list syntax stops at four methods.

choices.text: Two
choices.why: A list can hold more than a primary and a backup; the syntax allows method-1 through method-4.

choices.text: Four
choices.why: A method list is an ordered list of up to four AAA methods, tried from left to right.

questions.q: An organization uses Cisco ISE for AAA of network administrators and wants per-command control over what each administrator can run. Which protocol is most likely used between the routers and ISE?

choices.text: LDAP
choices.why: LDAP is a directory protocol that Duo can integrate with, but the router-to-ISE device administration protocol in the chapter is TACACS+.

choices.text: TACACS+
choices.why: For administrator AAA with ISE, TACACS+ is likely because it gives more granular control than RADIUS, including command authorization.

choices.text: SNMPv3
choices.why: SNMPv3 is an encrypted and authenticated management protocol for reading and changing device data. It is not used for AAA.

choices.text: RADIUS
choices.why: RADIUS is commonly used for network access, but it gives less granular control over administrator commands than TACACS+.

questions.q: An engineer has hard-coded a port with switchport mode access but notices DTP negotiation packets are still being sent. Which command stops them?

choices.text: spanning-tree bpduguard enable
choices.why: This enables BPDU Guard, which err-disables the port if a BPDU arrives. It does not stop DTP packets.

choices.text: switchport nonegotiate
choices.why: switchport nonegotiate disables DTP. DTP stays on by default even on a hard-coded access port until this command is entered.

choices.text: no cdp enable
choices.why: no cdp enable disables CDP on the interface, not DTP trunk negotiation.

choices.text: switchport trunk native vlan 3
choices.why: This sets an unused VLAN as a trunk's native VLAN. It does not disable DTP.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: In a router-on-a-stick design, which command on sub-interface Gi0/1.10 makes the router process frames tagged with VLAN 10?

choices.text: vlan 10 followed by state active
choices.why: These commands create and activate VLAN 10 in a switch's VLAN database. They don't map tags to a router sub-interface.

choices.text: switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
choices.why: This switch command sets 802.1Q as a trunk's encapsulation. On the router, the per-VLAN mapping is done with encapsulation dot1q on each sub-interface.

choices.text: switchport access vlan 10
choices.why: This is a switch command that places a Layer 2 access port in VLAN 10. It is not used on a router sub-interface.

choices.text: encapsulation dot1q 10
choices.why: encapsulation dot1q 10 tells the sub-interface to handle frames tagged with VLAN ID 10; the sub-interface number itself can be any value.

questions.q: Which statement about PortFast is correct?

choices.text: It is a Cisco enhancement that speeds recovery of uplinks after topology change
choices.why: That describes UplinkFast and BackboneFast, Cisco proprietary 802.1D improvements for faster convergence after a topology change.

choices.text: It err-disables a port that receives a BPDU
choices.why: Err-disabling a port on BPDU receipt is BPDU Guard, which is often paired with PortFast but is a separate feature.

choices.text: It skips listening and learning and should be used only on ports to a single host
choices.why: PortFast moves the port straight to forwarding, so it belongs only on ports to a single host; on hubs, switches, or bridges it risks a loop.

choices.text: It works only on 802.1Q trunk ports between switches
choices.why: The PortFast warning says it works only in non-trunking mode, and it is meant for host ports, not trunks between switches.

questions.q: A switch port connects to a partner's switch that your team does not manage. You want to make sure that switch can never become the root of your STP topology. Which command do you apply on that port?

choices.text: spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
choices.why: This global command changes the switch from 802.1D to 802.1w Rapid STP. It does not protect a port against a superior root.

choices.text: switchport port-security
choices.why: Port security limits how many MAC addresses a port can learn. It does not control the STP root election.

choices.text: spanning-tree portfast
choices.why: PortFast makes a port skip listening and learning. It offers no protection against a new root and is meant only for single-host ports.

choices.text: spanning-tree guard root
choices.why: Root Guard (spanning-tree guard root) stops the port from becoming a root port toward a new remote root switch, protecting the existing topology.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: An attacker sends thousands of frames with bogus source MAC addresses, and the switch begins flooding all frames to every port in the VLAN. Which feature is the primary mitigation?

choices.text: Root Guard
choices.why: Root Guard protects the STP topology from a new remote root switch. It doesn't limit MAC learning.

choices.text: Port security
choices.why: This is a CAM table overflow (MAC flooding) attack. Port security limits how many MACs a port can learn, so the table can't be filled.

choices.text: IP Source Guard
choices.why: IP Source Guard prevents spoofing of Layer 3 IP information. The flood of fake source MACs is a Layer 2 CAM issue.

choices.text: CoPP
choices.why: Control Plane Policing protects a router's CPU from traffic destined to the device. It does not protect a switch's CAM table.

questions.section: 6. Understanding and Securing the Data Plane

questions.q: After enabling DHCP snooping, which interface should be configured with ip dhcp snooping trust?

choices.text: The interface that connects to the legitimate DHCP server
choices.why: All ports are untrusted by default; the port toward the legitimate DHCP server must be trusted so its offers are forwarded without checks.

choices.text: Every access port that connects to end users
choices.why: User ports should stay untrusted so the switch validates their DHCP messages and blocks rogue DHCP servers.

choices.text: Any port where PortFast is enabled
choices.why: PortFast marks single-host ports, which are exactly the untrusted user ports DHCP snooping should inspect.

choices.text: The interface used for out-of-band management
choices.why: The management interface has nothing to do with DHCP snooping trust; only the path to the DHCP server needs trusting.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: Which command disables CDP on all interfaces of a device at once?

choices.text: no cdp enable
choices.why: no cdp enable disables CDP on a single interface only.

choices.text: no lldp run
choices.why: no lldp run disables LLDP globally, not CDP.

choices.text: no cdp run
choices.why: no cdp run disables CDP globally; show cdp then returns % CDP is not enabled.

choices.text: no service cdp
choices.why: This is not the IOS command. CDP is disabled globally with no cdp run.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: Which type of traffic belongs to the data plane?

choices.text: Transit traffic forwarded between clients and servers
choices.why: The data plane carries transit traffic that passes through the device between clients and servers.

choices.text: BGP updates received by the router
choices.why: BGP updates are control plane traffic destined to the router and handled by its route processor.

choices.text: SSH sessions from an administrator to the router
choices.why: Traffic between an administrator and the device itself is management plane traffic.

choices.text: OSPF hello packets between neighbors
choices.why: Routing protocol packets are control plane traffic that the device generates or receives itself.

questions.q: What does the service password-encryption command do?

choices.text: Locks accounts after repeated failed logins
choices.why: Account lockout is the Login Password Retry Lockout feature for local AAA users.

choices.text: Scrambles plaintext passwords in the configuration as type 7
choices.why: It scrambles plaintext passwords stored in the configuration, which then show as password 7. This mainly stops shoulder surfing.

choices.text: Hashes the privileged mode password as type 5
choices.why: The enable secret is hashed (shown as type 5). Service password encryption only applies weak type 7 scrambling to plaintext passwords.

choices.text: Enforces a minimum length on new passwords
choices.why: Minimum length is enforced by security passwords min-length, not service password-encryption.

questions.q: With Login Password Retry Lockout configured, a local AAA user exceeds the allowed number of failed login attempts. What happens?

choices.text: The account is locked until an administrator unlocks it
choices.why: The feature locks the local AAA account after the configured number of failures, and only an administrator can unlock it.

choices.text: The vty line is moved to the parking-lot VLAN
choices.why: A parking-lot VLAN holds unused switch ports. It has nothing to do with failed login attempts.

choices.text: The account unlocks automatically after 30 seconds
choices.why: There is no automatic unlock; 30 seconds is the errdisable recovery interval in the BPDU Guard example.

choices.text: The user is dropped to privilege level 1
choices.why: Lockout prevents login entirely; it doesn't place the user at a lower privilege level.

questions.q: What does SNMPv3 add compared with SNMP versions 1 and 2c?

choices.text: YANG data models in place of the MIB
choices.why: YANG models are used by NETCONF, RESTCONF, and gNMI. SNMP still uses its MIB tree.

choices.text: Transport over SSH instead of UDP
choices.why: NETCONF runs over SSH. SNMPv3 secures its messages itself rather than moving to SSH.

choices.text: Proper encryption and authentication
choices.why: Versions 1 and 2c lack proper encryption and authentication; version 3 adds both, which is why the book recommends it.

choices.text: Atomic transactions with rollback
choices.why: Atomic commit-or-rollback transactions are a NETCONF feature. SNMP has no built-in transactions.

questions.q: Which logging destination stores messages in router memory, rotates them first in first out, and loses them on reboot?

choices.text: A syslog server
choices.why: A syslog server receives and stores a large volume of messages externally, so they survive a router reboot.

choices.text: An SNMP server
choices.why: An SNMP server receives log messages sent as SNMP traps over the network rather than storing them in router memory.

choices.text: The startup configuration in NVRAM
choices.why: NVRAM holds the startup configuration and survives reboots. Log messages are not stored there.

choices.text: The logging buffer
choices.why: The logging buffer keeps messages in router memory up to the configured size, rotated FIFO, and they are lost on reboot.

questions.q: An attacker spoofs the source IP address of your NTP server to send false time to your routers. What prevents this?

choices.text: service timestamps log datetime
choices.why: This adds date and time to syslog messages. It does nothing to authenticate time sources.

choices.text: NTP authentication with a trusted key
choices.why: NTP authentication (ntp authenticate, an authentication key, and ntp trusted-key) stops a rogue server with a spoofed source IP from changing your time.

choices.text: ntp update-calendar
choices.why: ntp update-calendar only updates the hardware calendar from NTP. It doesn't verify the server.

choices.text: Pointing the router at a lower stratum server
choices.why: Stratum relates to distance from the reference clock. A spoofed server can still send false time unless authentication is used.

questions.q: After Cisco Resilient Configuration is enabled with secure boot-image and secure boot-config, how can it be disabled?

choices.text: By reloading the router twice
choices.why: Reloads don't remove the secure bootset. The no commands must be issued from the console.

choices.text: Only from the console with the no forms of the commands
choices.why: Once enabled, Resilient Configuration can't be disabled remotely; no secure boot-image and no secure boot-config work only from the console.

choices.text: By deleting the .ar archive from flash
choices.why: The secure archive can't be deleted by a remote user; that is how it protects the startup configuration.

choices.text: From any SSH session at privilege level 15
choices.why: Remote sessions can't disable it, even at level 15, which is the point of protecting the bootset from remote attackers.

questions.q: How many bits long is an IPv6 address?

choices.why: 64 bits is the usual size of the interface ID or the network ID portion, not the whole address.
32 bits is the size of an IPv4 address.
48 bits is the size of a MAC address, which modified EUI-64 expands to a 64-bit interface ID.
An IPv6 address is 128 bits (16 bytes), written as eight groups of four hex characters.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: Which IPv6 multicast group is joined by routers that have IPv6 routing enabled?

choices.why: FF02::2 is the all-routers multicast address, equivalent to IPv4 224.0.0.2.

choices.text: FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx
choices.why: FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx is the solicited-node range, joined for each unicast and anycast address on any device.
FF02::9 is the RIPng multicast group, like 224.0.0.9 for RIPv2.
FF02::1 is all-nodes multicast, joined by every IPv6 device.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: Control Plane Protection (CPPr) divides control plane traffic into sub-interfaces. Which one handles network operations traffic such as keepalives and packets with expiring TTL?

choices.text: CEF exception sub-interface
choices.why: The CEF exception sub-interface handles network operations traffic such as keepalives and packets whose TTL is expiring.

choices.text: Host sub-interface
choices.why: The host sub-interface handles traffic destined to one of the router's own physical or logical interfaces.

choices.text: Transit sub-interface
choices.why: The transit sub-interface handles data plane traffic that needs CPU help before forwarding, such as packets with IP options.

choices.text: Punt sub-interface
choices.why: CPPr has only host, transit, and CEF exception sub-interfaces. The punt path is the path from forwarding hardware to the route processor.

questions.q: Which single command enables MD5 authentication with BGP neighbor 192.168.10.2 in the book's example?

choices.text: ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 LAB
choices.why: This configures an OSPF MD5 key on an interface, not BGP.

choices.text: ip authentication key-chain bgp 65000 LAB
choices.why: The ip authentication key-chain form is EIGRP interface syntax (ip authentication key-chain eigrp). It isn't how BGP MD5 is set in the example.

choices.text: neighbor 192.168.10.2 password LAB-SECURITY
choices.why: BGP MD5 needs only the neighbor password option under router bgp; the peer needs a similar configuration.

choices.text: neighbor 192.168.10.2 remote-as 65100
choices.why: This defines the BGP peer and its AS. It is part of the base setup and adds no authentication.

questions.section: 12. Securing Routing Protocols and the Control Plane

questions.q: Why should IPv6 Routing Header type 0 (RH0) packets be dropped?

choices.text: They are always encrypted with IPsec
choices.why: RH0 is a routing extension header, not an encryption mechanism. IPsec is supported in IPv6 but not required.

choices.text: They tunnel IPv6 inside IPv4 automatically
choices.why: Automatic IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling describes mechanisms such as 6to4, not the routing header.

choices.text: They let an attacker dictate the path, like IP source routing
choices.why: RH0 lists intermediate nodes the packet must pass, so an attacker can dictate the path and even loop packets until TTL expires.

choices.text: They carry rogue router advertisements
choices.why: Rogue router advertisements are ND messages that RA Guard blocks. They are not RH0 extension headers.

questions.q: What distinguishes a brute-force password attack from a dictionary attack?

choices.text: It forges ARP replies to intercept login traffic
choices.why: Forged ARP replies describe ARP spoofing, a man-in-the-middle technique, not a password guessing attack.

choices.text: It tries a long list of words one after another
choices.why: Working through a list of words is a dictionary attack, not brute force.

choices.text: It tries every possible character string up to a set length

questions.q: What is the most important field in an 802.1Q tag?

choices.text: The bridge ID
choices.why: The bridge ID (priority plus MAC) is used in STP BPDUs to elect the root bridge, not in the 802.1Q tag.

choices.text: The VLAN ID
choices.why: The 802.1Q tag tells the receiving switch which VLAN the frame belongs to, so the VLAN ID is the key field.

choices.text: The port priority
choices.why: Port priority is an STP value used to break ties between equal-cost ports. It is not carried in the 802.1Q tag.

choices.text: The native VLAN number
choices.why: Native VLAN frames are sent untagged, so the native VLAN is not a field in the tag.

questions.q: By default, which VLANs does show interface trunk list as allowed on an 802.1Q trunk?

choices.why: Trunks allow VLANs 1 through 4094 by default.
2-1001 is the default range of pruning-eligible VLANs shown in show interfaces switchport, not the allowed range.
VLANs 1002 to 1005 are the built-in default VLANs (fddi-default, token-ring-default, and others), not the allowed list.

choices.text: Only the native VLAN
choices.why: A trunk carries many VLANs; the native VLAN is just the one sent untagged.

questions.q: Show spanning-tree vlan 10 reports a bridge priority of 32778 even though the default priority was never changed. Why?

choices.text: The switch adds its port cost of 10 to the priority
choices.why: Port cost (19 in the examples) is used for path cost to the root and is not added to the bridge priority.

choices.text: The system ID extension adds the VLAN number to 32768
choices.why: The default priority is 32768, and the system ID extension adds the VLAN number, so VLAN 10 shows 32768 + 10 = 32778.

choices.text: Rapid PVST+ raises the default priority by 10
choices.why: Switching to rapid-pvst changes the protocol to 802.1w but does not change how the priority is shown.

choices.text: Root Guard increases the priority to stay non-root
choices.why: Root Guard blocks a port from becoming a root port toward a new root. It does not alter the bridge priority value.

choices.text: Two, one per trunk
choices.why: STP instances are created per VLAN, not per trunk link.

choices.text: Zero until spanning tree is enabled
choices.why: STP is on by default on most Cisco switches, so instances run without extra configuration.

choices.text: Five, one per VLAN
choices.why: PVST+ is Cisco's default and runs a separate STP instance for each VLAN, so five VLANs mean five instances.

questions.q: An engineer wants a port that exceeds its MAC limit to stay up, drop frames from the extra MACs, and generate a syslog message. Which violation mode should be configured?

choices.text: Shutdown

choices.text: Protect

choices.text: Sticky
choices.why: Sticky is not a violation mode; it writes learned MAC addresses into the running configuration.

choices.text: FF02::1 followed by the full 64-bit interface ID

choices.text: FF02::2 followed by the router's MAC address

choices.text: FF02::1:FF followed by the last 24 bits of the host ID
choices.why: The solicited-node address is FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx, where the x values are the last 24 bits of the unicast or anycast address.

choices.text: FE80:: followed by the modified EUI-64 interface ID
choices.why: That is how a link-local unicast address is formed, not a solicited-node multicast.

choices.text: The prefix is forwarded in hardware without the CPU

choices.text: Packets to that address are for the device itself and go to the CPU
choices.why: A receive adjacency covers the device's own interface IPs plus multicast and broadcast addresses; these packets hit the control plane and CPU.

choices.text: Packets to that address are dropped by Unicast RPF
choices.why: Unicast RPF drops packets whose source isn't reachable via the incoming interface; it is not what receive means in CEF.

questions.q: A switch logs that the same source MAC address keeps being relearned on two different ports. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: CDP advertisements to a multicast address
choices.why: CDP advertises device details to a multicast address. These advertisements don't cause MAC flapping.

choices.text: A Layer 2 loop between switches with parallel links
choices.why: MAC address flapping happens when a looping frame arrives on both ports, a classic symptom of a Layer 2 loop that STP should prevent.

choices.text: An expired DHCP snooping binding
choices.why: DHCP snooping bindings record leased IPs on untrusted ports. An expired binding doesn't make a MAC appear on two ports.

choices.text: A port security violation in protect mode
choices.why: Protect mode quietly drops frames from MACs over the limit. It does not cause a MAC to move between ports.

choices.text: errdisable recovery cause bpduguard and errdisable recovery interval 30
choices.why: The cause command enables automatic recovery for BPDU Guard, and the interval command brings ports back after 30 seconds without a violation.

choices.why: Shutdown then no shutdown recovers an err-disabled port manually, not automatically.

choices.why: These are verification commands showing recovery causes, timers, and port status. They change nothing.

choices.text: DHCP snooping

questions.q: How does a control plane failure affect the data plane?

questions.q: How does access control in SNMP versions 1 and 2c compare with the access control used by NETCONF?

choices.text: SNMP uses TACACS+ for each request; NETCONF uses RADIUS
choices.why: Neither protocol's built-in access control is TACACS+ or RADIUS; they are community strings and NACM.

choices.text: Both rely on per-object community strings
choices.why: Community strings are not per object; they cover the whole tree, and NETCONF does not use them.

choices.why: NETCONF doesn't use SNMP, and a failed transaction is not kept.

choices.text: The device retries the failed change until it succeeds
choices.why: Atomic transactions don't retry. They commit everything or roll everything back.

choices.text: The first six changes stay and the rest are skipped
choices.why: That would be a partial update, which atomic transactions are designed to prevent.

choices.text: The entire set of changes is rolled back
choices.why: An atomic transaction is either fully committed or entirely rolled back on error, avoiding partial or inconsistent updates.

questions.q: What is the IPv6 loopback address?

choices.why: FF02::1 is the all-nodes multicast address, joined by every IPv6 device.
FE80 addresses are link-local unicast, used on the local network, not the loopback.
The IPv6 loopback is ::1, which is 127 zeros followed by a 1. IPv4 uses the 127 range.
127 is the IPv4 loopback range; IPv6 does not use a 127 prefix for loopback.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: A router has IPv6 addresses on two interfaces and can ping from both, but hosts on one segment can't reach the other through it. Which command lets the router forward other devices' IPv6 packets?

choices.text: ipv6 traffic-filter IPv6-ACL in
choices.why: This applies an IPv6 ACL inbound on an interface. It filters traffic but doesn't enable forwarding.

choices.text: ipv6 ospf 1 area 0
choices.why: This enables OSPFv3 on an interface to exchange routes; it doesn't turn on IPv6 packet forwarding.

choices.text: ipv6 router eigrp 1 then no shutdown
choices.why: This brings the EIGRP for IPv6 process out of shutdown, but forwarding itself requires ipv6 unicast-routing.

choices.text: ipv6 unicast-routing
choices.why: Without ipv6 unicast-routing a router only sends and receives its own IPv6 packets; this command enables forwarding.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: Why does a packet arriving with a TTL of 1 add load to a router's CPU?

choices.text: The router must fragment the packet before forwarding
choices.why: Fragmentation is another CPU-processed case, but it is triggered by MTU, not by TTL expiry.

choices.text: The router must generate an ICMP Time Exceeded (Type 11, Code 0) reply
choices.why: Packets with TTL 1 or less need an ICMP Type 11, Code 0 Time Exceeded message, which is CPU-processed.

choices.text: The router must send an ARP request for the destination
choices.why: ARP requests are needed for destinations with no ARP entry. TTL expiry triggers ICMP Time Exceeded instead.

choices.text: The router must log the packet because of the ACL log keyword
choices.why: ACL logging is CPU-processed only for packets matching an ACE with log, unrelated to TTL.

questions.section: 12. Securing Routing Protocols and the Control Plane

questions.q: Which CPPr feature polices and drops packets sent to closed or nonlistening TCP or UDP ports?

choices.text: TCP Intercept
choices.why: TCP Intercept reduces the risk of SYN-flood attacks; it doesn't drop traffic to closed ports in the control plane.

choices.text: Queue-thresholding feature
choices.why: Queue thresholding limits how many packets of a given protocol can sit in the control plane IP input queue.

choices.text: Selective Packet Discard
choices.why: SPD prioritizes critical packets such as routing updates and keepalives to the route processor; it isn't the closed-port filter.

choices.text: Port-filtering feature
choices.why: CPPr's port-filtering feature polices and drops packets destined to closed or nonlistening TCP or UDP ports.

questions.section: 12. Securing Routing Protocols and the Control Plane

questions.q: A company with 50 VLANs needs inter-VLAN routing but doesn't want to use 50 router interfaces and 50 switch ports. Which design solves this?

choices.text: Putting all users in VLAN 1 to avoid routing
choices.why: VLAN 1 should be avoided, and one broadcast domain for hundreds of users defeats the point of separating groups into subnets.

choices.text: One router interface per VLAN connected to access ports
choices.why: This works but doesn't scale; 50 VLANs would need 50 router interfaces and 50 switch ports.

choices.text: Making the native VLAN the default gateway on each trunk
choices.why: The native VLAN only carries untagged frames on a trunk; inter-VLAN routing always needs a Layer 3 device as the gateway.

choices.text: Router-on-a-stick with one sub-interface per VLAN over a trunk
choices.why: Router-on-a-stick trunks one physical router interface to the switch and maps each VLAN tag to its own sub-interface with an IP address.

questions.q: Which statement describes an STP root port?

choices.text: The port closest to the root bridge by path cost; every non-root switch has exactly one
choices.why: The root port receives the best BPDU on the switch, being closest to the root by STP path cost, and each non-root switch has exactly one.

choices.text: A port that doesn't forward packets so that no loop forms
choices.why: That is a nondesignated port, shown as Altn BLK in the book's output.

choices.text: Every port on the root bridge itself
choices.why: All ports on the root bridge forward for its VLAN, but the root bridge has no root port.

choices.text: The port on a segment that can send the best BPDU for a VLAN
choices.why: That describes a designated port, chosen per segment.

questions.q: SW2 receives BPDUs from SW1 on ports 23 and 24 with equal path cost to the root. How does SW2 decide which port to block?

choices.text: It keeps the port with the higher port priority
choices.why: In STP lower is always preferred, so the higher value loses.

choices.text: It blocks whichever port came up first
choices.why: Port startup order isn't an STP tie-breaker; sender port priority is used.

choices.text: It forwards on both ports and lets BPDU Guard shut one
choices.why: Forwarding on both would create a loop, and BPDU Guard is meant for access ports, not inter-switch links.

choices.text: It compares the sender's port priority and keeps the lower value, blocking the other port
choices.why: With equal cost, SW2 uses the sender's port priority and picks the lower value; lower-numbered ports have lower priorities by default, so port 24 blocks.

questions.q: After an engineer enters spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst, what change appears in show spanning-tree output?

choices.text: The bridge priority changes to 0
choices.why: The mode change doesn't alter the bridge priority, which stays 32768 plus the VLAN number by default.

choices.text: All ports show as PortFast edge ports
choices.why: Changing the STP mode doesn't enable PortFast; that requires spanning-tree portfast or portfast default.

choices.text: The protocol shows as mstp instead of ieee
choices.why: MST is not covered by this command. rapid-pvst makes the output show rstp.

choices.text: The protocol shows as rstp instead of ieee
choices.why: rapid-pvst switches from 802.1D to 802.1w, and the output then says protocol rstp instead of ieee.

questions.q: A user's access port connects an IP phone with a built-in switch, a PC, and a couple of virtual machines, and port security keeps triggering. What should the engineer change?

choices.text: Enable spanning-tree bpduguard enable
choices.why: BPDU Guard reacts to BPDUs, not to the number of MAC addresses, so it won't fix the violations.

choices.text: Raise the limit with switchport port-security maximum
choices.why: The default maximum is 1 MAC; legitimate extras such as VMs or a phone need a higher limit, for example switchport port-security maximum 5.

choices.text: Configure ip dhcp snooping trust on the port
choices.why: Trusting the port for DHCP snooping is for the DHCP server link; it doesn't change the port security MAC limit.

choices.text: Apply switchport trunk native vlan 3
choices.why: This sets a trunk's native VLAN and has no effect on port security limits on an access port.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: What is the purpose of ip dhcp snooping database tftp://10.1.1.1/directory/file?

choices.text: It downloads a list of authorized DHCP servers
choices.why: Authorized servers are defined by trusting the interface toward them, not by a downloaded file.

choices.text: It backs up the startup configuration as a secure archive
choices.why: A secure configuration archive is Cisco Resilient Configuration (secure boot-config), not DHCP snooping.

choices.text: It stores the bindings so they are restored after a restart or switchover
choices.why: The database agent saves DHCP snooping bindings externally so the entries survive a switch restart or switchover.

choices.text: It sends DHCP snooping violations to a syslog server
choices.why: Syslog messages go to syslog servers over UDP 514; this command saves the binding database to a TFTP URL.

questions.section: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them

questions.q: An engineer enters ip dhcp snooping globally, but show ip dhcp snooping shows no VLANs being snooped. What else is needed?

choices.text: Mark all user ports with ip dhcp snooping trust
choices.why: User ports should remain untrusted; only the port toward the DHCP server is trusted.

choices.text: Enable ip arp inspection vlan 10
choices.why: This enables DAI on VLAN 10, which relies on DHCP snooping, but it doesn't enable snooping on the VLAN.

choices.text: Disable DTP with switchport nonegotiate
choices.why: Disabling DTP stops trunk negotiation, which is unrelated to activating DHCP snooping on a VLAN.

choices.text: Enable snooping on at least one VLAN, such as ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
choices.why: DHCP snooping is enabled per VLAN and is inactive on all VLANs by default, so at least one VLAN or range must be specified.

questions.q: Which discovery protocol extension was designed for media endpoint devices such as voice equipment?

choices.text: CDP version 2
choices.why: CDP is Cisco's proprietary discovery protocol from 1994. The named extension for media endpoints is LLDP-MED.

choices.text: DTP
choices.why: DTP negotiates whether a port becomes an access port or a trunk; it is not a discovery protocol.

choices.text: LLDP-MED
choices.why: LLDP-MED, LLDP for Media Endpoint Devices, is the voice-oriented extension of the IEEE LLDP standard.

choices.text: PVST+
choices.why: PVST+ is Cisco's per-VLAN spanning tree, not a discovery protocol.

questions.q: What does the command privilege exec level 8 configure terminal do?

choices.text: Moves the configure terminal command down to privilege level 8
choices.why: This creates a custom level by moving configure terminal from level 15 to level 8, so level 8 users can enter configuration mode.

choices.text: Sets the password used to enter privilege level 8
choices.why: The level 8 password is set with enable secret level 8; the privilege command assigns commands to a level.

choices.text: Places a user at level 8 every time he logs in
choices.why: That is done with username ... privilege 8 secret ..., which assigns the level to an account.

choices.text: Creates a parser view named level 8
choices.why: Parser views are created with parser view <name> from the root view, not with the privilege command.

questions.q: In the command enable secret level 8 0 NewPa5s123&, what does the 0 mean?

choices.text: The password that follows is typed unhashed and will be hashed
choices.why: The 0 means you are entering the password in clear form, and the secret keyword hashes it.

choices.text: The account has zero failed login attempts allowed
choices.why: Failed login limits belong to Login Password Retry Lockout, not to enable secret syntax.

choices.text: The password applies to privilege level 0
choices.why: The level is set by level 8; the 0 describes how the password is entered.

choices.text: The password is stored in type 7 form
choices.why: Type 7 is the weak scrambling from service password-encryption; the secret keyword hashes the password instead.

questions.q: A router uses command authorization with group tacacs+ local. The TACACS+ (ISE) server becomes unreachable while an administrator is working. What does the router do before each command?

choices.text: It allows every command with no checks
choices.why: Allowing everything would require the none method, which isn't in this list.

choices.text: It checks the user's privilege level in the local database
choices.why: With the local method listed after group tacacs+, the router falls back to the local database when the server can't be reached.

choices.text: It uses the enable secret to approve each command
choices.why: The enable method isn't in this authorization list; the fallback is the local database.

choices.text: It rejects every command until the server returns
choices.why: Rejection would happen only with no fallback method; local is listed as the second method.

questions.q: BGP MD5 authentication originally placed its digest in TCP option Kind 19. Which RFC created that option?

choices.text: RFC 2328
choices.why: RFC 2328 defines OSPF version 2, not the TCP option used for BGP MD5 signatures.

choices.text: RFC 5925
choices.why: RFC 5925 defines TCP-AO, option Kind 29, which obsoleted the Kind 19 MD5 option.

choices.text: RFC 2385
choices.why: RFC 2385 created TCP option Kind 19, the MD5 Signature Option, which has since been obsoleted by option Kind 29.

choices.text: RFC 4253
choices.why: RFC 4253, section 5.1, covers SSH version 1.99 backward compatibility.

questions.q: Which Duo capability checks the posture of a device before granting access?

choices.text: Generic RADIUS integration
choices.why: Generic RADIUS is one way Duo integrates with applications; it doesn't by itself check device posture.

choices.text: The user enrollment strategy
choices.why: The enrollment strategy shapes Duo policy but doesn't perform device posture checks.

choices.text: The Trusted Endpoints policy in Duo Beyond
choices.why: Duo Beyond adds a Trusted Endpoints policy that checks device posture.

choices.text: A per-application SAML configuration
choices.why: SAML configurations connect Duo to applications, but posture checking is the Trusted Endpoints policy.

questions.q: In show ntp association output, which symbol marks the server the router is actually synchronized to (sys.peer)?

choices.why: The pound sign marks a selected server, not the sys.peer.
The asterisk marks the sys.peer, the server the router is synchronized to.
The plus sign marks a candidate server.

choices.text: x
choices.why: The x marks a falseticker, a server whose time is considered wrong.

questions.q: A router logs %LINK-3-UPDOWN after an interface goes down. What severity is this message?

choices.text: Level 2, Critical
choices.why: Level 2 is Critical, one level more severe than the 3 in this message.

choices.text: Level 6, Informational
choices.why: Level 6 is Informational; the message clearly carries level 3.

choices.text: Level 5, Notifications
choices.why: Level 5 Notifications appears in %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN, not %LINK-3-UPDOWN.

choices.text: Level 3, Error
choices.why: The number after the facility is the severity, and level 3 is Error (error conditions).

questions.q: How does Unicast RPF decide to drop a packet?

choices.text: The packet's source address wouldn't be reachable out the interface it arrived on
choices.why: Unicast RPF checks the source: if the route back to that source doesn't use the incoming interface, the packet is dropped as likely spoofed.

choices.text: The packet's destination has no entry in the CEF table
choices.why: Unicast RPF checks the source address, not the destination.

choices.text: The packet exceeds the CoPP police rate
choices.why: Exceeding a CoPP police rate drops traffic to the control plane; that is policing, not reverse path checking.

choices.text: The packet arrives with a TTL of 1 or less
choices.why: TTL expiry triggers an ICMP Time Exceeded reply; it isn't the Unicast RPF check.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares IPv6 with IPv4?

choices.text: IPv6 relies on NAT to stretch its address space
choices.why: IPv4 uses NAT; IPv6 doesn't support NAT by design because it has plenty of addresses.

choices.text: IPv6 uses multicast and Neighbor Discovery instead of broadcasts and ARP
choices.why: IPv6 has no broadcasts and no ARP; it uses multicast and ND, which also discovers the network address and routers.

choices.text: IPv6 replaces TCP and UDP with new transport protocols
choices.why: TCP and UDP stay the same in both versions; the big change is at Layer 3.

choices.text: IPv6 requires IPsec on every packet
choices.why: IPsec is fully supported in IPv6 and was supposed to be mandatory, but IPv6 doesn't actually require it.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: A team must carry IPv6 across an IPv4-only section of the network. Following the chapter's best practice, which tunnel approach should they use?

choices.text: 6to4 automatic tunnels
choices.why: 6to4 is an automatic mechanism the book says to avoid, because automatic tunnels are dynamic and hard to control.

choices.text: Manual tunnels that don't cross the perimeter
choices.why: The book recommends manual tunnels, not automatic ones, and says not to let tunnels cross your perimeter since their contents are hard to control.

choices.text: Any tunnel, since the IPv4 network inspects the inner IPv6 packets
choices.why: The IPv4 network may not inspect IPv6 packets inside a tunnel, which is why filtering at the tunnel edges is needed.

choices.text: Automatic tunnels terminated outside the firewall
choices.why: Automatic tunnels should be avoided, and tunnels should not cross the perimeter.

questions.section: 11. Securing the Data Plane in IPv6

questions.q: Secure Neighbor Discovery (SeND) adds new ND options and which two new messages?

choices.text: Neighbor solicitation and neighbor advertisement
choices.why: NS and NA are the standard ND request and reply, which existed before SeND.

choices.text: Router solicitation and router advertisement
choices.why: These are standard ND router discovery messages, not the additions made by SeND.

choices.text: Certification Path Solicitation and Certification Path Answer
choices.why: SeND adds the CPS and CPA messages, along with new ND options, to counter ND spoofing and redirection.

choices.text: SubscribeRequest and SubscribeResponse
choices.why: These are gNMI messages from the book's Protocol Buffers example, unrelated to ND.

choices.text: aes128-cbc and hmac-sha1

choices.text: Plaintext and MD5
choices.why: Plaintext and MD5 are the options for RIPv2 and OSPF, not the BGP algorithm list.
